items.prompt: What does "queueing theory" study, per this unit?
choices: How to design user interfaces for waiting screens
What happens when requests arrive at a system faster than, or comparably close to, the rate the system can process them
How to write faster sorting algorithms
The history of line-waiting customs in different cultures
items.reference: 📊 Queueing theory — arrivals vs. processing capacity
items.explanation: Queueing theory studies what happens when requests arrive at a system faster than, or comparably close to, the rate the system can process them — the mathematics behind waiting lines, whether for checkout registers or API requests.

items.prompt: According to this unit, what kinds of "requests" can queueing theory apply to?
choices: Only literal human customers in a physical line
Requests, customers, packets, or anything else that arrives at a system needing processing
Only HTTP requests specifically
Only requests measured in whole numbers, never fractional rates
items.reference: 📊 Queueing theory — arrivals vs. processing capacity
items.explanation: The unit is explicit that queueing theory applies broadly — requests, customers, packets, or anything else arriving at a system that needs processing, not just literal human lines.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "utilization" (ρ)?
choices: The total number of servers a system has
The fraction of a system's maximum processing capacity currently being used — arrival rate divided by service rate
The percentage of requests that fail
The average size of a request in bytes
items.reference:
📏 Utilization (ρ) — arrival rate ÷ service rate
⚠️ Must stay below 1 for stability
items.explanation: Utilization is the fraction of a system's maximum processing capacity currently in use, computed as arrival rate divided by service rate (ρ = λ / μ) — a system at 60% utilization is using 60% of its maximum throughput.

items.prompt: What must be true of utilization for a queue to remain stable in the long run, per this unit?
choices: It must always equal exactly 1
It must stay below 1
It must always be a whole number
Stability doesn't depend on utilization at all
items.reference:
📏 Utilization (ρ) — arrival rate ÷ service rate
⚠️ Must stay below 1 for stability
items.explanation: Utilization must stay below 1 for a queue to remain stable — if arrivals equal or exceed service capacity indefinitely, the queue grows without bound rather than settling into a steady state.

items.prompt: What does Little's Law state, per this unit?
choices: The average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends in the system (L = λW)
All queues eventually become infinitely long
The service rate always equals the arrival rate
Utilization is always exactly 50%
items.reference:
🧮 Little's Law — L = λW
🌍 Holds for almost any stable queueing system
items.explanation: Little's Law states that the average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends there — a simple, general relationship written as L = λW.

items.prompt: What makes Little's Law useful as a "sanity check" on capacity planning, per this unit?
choices: It only applies to a single, very specific type of queue
It holds for almost any queueing system regardless of the specific arrival or service pattern
It requires knowing the exact probability distribution of every request
It can only be verified through expensive real-world experiments
items.reference:
🧮 Little's Law — L = λW
🌍 Holds for almost any stable queueing system
items.explanation: Little's Law's generality is what makes it useful — it holds for almost any stable queueing system regardless of the specific arrival or service pattern, so it works as a cross-check even without knowing detailed distributional assumptions.

⏱️ Latency — time per individual request
items.explanation: Throughput measures how much work a system completes per unit time, while latency measures how long any individual request takes — the two are related but not interchangeable, and a system can have high throughput and terrible latency simultaneously.
